summary:
Kano stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, for all persons including visitors. Over that national layer, Kano State operates its own religious penal code, the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, which took effect on 26 November 2000.

The statutory ceiling in Kano is the harshest available to a trans visitor in the country. Under the Kano Sharia Penal Code, consensual same-sex activity draws 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment where the offender is unmarried, and stoning to death (rajm) where the offender is or has been married. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression and sex characteristics in Nigeria (June 2025) reproduces the same comparison: the Kano code prescribes death by stoning for married or previously married men, and 100 lashes with imprisonment of up to one year for unmarried men. The note confirms that the codes remain in force.

The exposure is not confined to men. The Home Office note records Kano's capital maximum for the offence termed 'lesbianism' as death, alongside Katsina; the other ten states operating Sharia codes punish the same conduct by flogging and up to six months' imprisonment. It also records that Kano's capital maximum applies to same-sex acts between women as well as between men.

Gender expression carries its own criminal exposure. Kano's separate Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law criminalises cross-dressing by men, so attire and presentation are themselves matters of criminal law in the state.

Enforcement is documented, not theoretical. In 2023, eight people convicted of wearing female clothing at a wedding were reportedly flogged in public on Hisbah premises in Kano state. The Hisbah, the state religious police, are recorded in the US Commission on International Religious Freedom's 2019 study of Sharia criminal-law implementation as the most active command among the states surveyed; that study drew on 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 in Kano, Sokoto and Zamfara and recorded Hisbah activity in each.

Nigeria-wide context applies on top of this. The SSMPA criminalises not only same-sex conduct but cohabitation between same-sex partners, public displays of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years, and police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. Human Rights Watch and the Thomson Reuters Foundation document police extortion of people stopped for looking gay and kito gangs that lure victims through dating apps to meetings where they are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail, imprisonment of up to 14 years and the death-penalty risk under Sharia law in the northern states.
tangentialFactors:
Across the twelve Nigerian states operating Sharia codes, penalties for the same conduct are not uniform. Kano and Katsina set death as the maximum for conduct termed 'lesbianism'; the other ten states impose flogging and up to six months' imprisonment. A visitor's exposure therefore changes materially on crossing state lines, and Kano sits at the severe end of that range.

Public corporal punishment has been carried out in Kano on religious-police premises. The 2023 flogging of eight people for wearing female clothing at a wedding indicates that gender-nonconforming presentation is punished visibly and on state property, not only through court sentences.

The trans-specific imprisonment case in the Nigerian sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), sentenced on 12 April 2024 to six months for naira abuse and held in a maximum-security prison in Lagos; an October 2024 panel found that housing her there breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act. Press coverage at sentencing openly debated which prison would hold a crossdresser, indicating that placement between male and female sections is left to official discretion. Kano state institutions present a markedly less favourable setting for such discretionary placement than Lagos, though the sources available here do not document a Kano-specific placement case.

On cross-dressing: Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians feared proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing, but whether any such proposal has been enacted is not settled by the sources available. Kano does not depend on such a proposal, since its own Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law already criminalises cross-dressing by men.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kano are subject to the state's Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law, which criminalises cross-dressing by men independently of the national Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014.

The Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, in force since 26 November 2000, is the operative penal framework for same-sex conduct in the state. It prescribes 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment for unmarried offenders, and stoning to death for offenders who are or have been married.

The Hisbah is the state's religious police and is recorded by USCIRF as the most active Hisbah command among the states surveyed. Residents report stop-and-arrest encounters with the Hisbah in their own communities; enforcement includes public corporal punishment on Hisbah premises, as in the 2023 case of eight people flogged for wearing female clothing at a wedding.

For women, the Kano maximum penalty under the code for conduct termed 'lesbianism' is death, a ceiling shared with Katsina and absent from the ten other states operating Sharia codes, which impose flogging and up to six months' imprisonment.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people. The national framework supplies no hate-crime protection, no protection from housing or employment discrimination, and no recognition of same-sex partnerships; the SSMPA additionally criminalises cohabitation between same-sex partners, public display of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations.

Extortion and violence are documented features of enforcement. Police officers have been recorded demanding bribes from men stopped on suspicion of being gay, and LGBTQ+ Nigerians report extortion through dating-app entrapment by gangs who beat, film and blackmail victims with threats of outing.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted at federal level is unresolved by the sources available here. For Kano the question is partly moot, because the state's own Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law already criminalises cross-dressing by men; the sources do not state whether that state law distinguishes between residents and visitors in its application.

The sources do not state how the Kano Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law interacts with the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, or whether charges are typically brought under one, the other, or both.

No Kano-specific case of a trans person in state custody, of document or marker rules for trans travellers at entry, or of access to gender-affirming healthcare in Kano appears in the sources available. The Bobrisky imprisonment case is documented for Lagos, not Kano.

Whether stoning sentences under the Kano Sharia Penal Code have been carried out, as distinct from imposed, is not established by the sources available here.

The June 2025 Home Office note confirms the Sharia codes remain in force, but the sources available do not document recent Hisbah enforcement activity in Kano after 2023.
